subject: Surgery
summary: Enteral feeding is the preferred route when the gut is functional, started early to preserve mucosa and reduce complications. It requires careful assessment of contraindications and monitoring for intolerance.

sections.p: Enteral feeding (EN) delivers nutrients directly into the gastrointestinal tract, usually via nasogastric, nasojejunal, or gastrostomy tubes. Diagnosis is clinical: the patient is unable to meet nutritional needs orally but has a functional gut.
b: EN is indicated when oral intake <50% of requirements for >48h
EN is contraindicated if bowel is non‑functional or obstructed

sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of nutritional deficit and the presence of complications such as aspiration or tube misplacement.
Common reasons for EN in low‑resource hospitals include postoperative ileus, trauma, burns, and severe infections where oral intake is unsafe.
Patients may show abdominal distension, vomiting, or inability to tolerate oral feeds. Signs of intolerance include high gastric residuals, abdominal pain, or diarrhea.

t.b: Detects tube position, obstruction, or perforation; misplacement can cause pneumoperitoneum
Monitors electrolytes, renal function, and acid–base status; derangements may limit feeding
Identifies anemia that may worsen tolerance
Assesses inflammatory status; high CRP may delay initiation

sections.p: Urgent signs include sudden abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, or signs of sepsis. Complications can be mechanical (tube dislodgement), infectious (aspiration pneumonia), or metabolic (electrolyte imbalance).

Treat the underlying cause first, then initiate EN at 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing by 10–20 % daily. Use thiamine supplementation to prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Monitor for intolerance and adjust as needed.
b: Use proton pump inhibitor if reflux suspected
Avoid NSAIDs if renal failure or GI bleed

sections.p: Regularly assess weight, serum albumin, and caloric intake. Prevent complications by ensuring proper tube placement, monitoring residuals, and early mobilization.
Enteral feeding is often mistaken for total parenteral nutrition (TPN) or oral feeding. Unlike TPN, EN preserves gut integrity and is cheaper.
b: TPN – intravenous route, higher infection risk

sections.p: Low albumin may reflect inflammation rather than malnutrition; normal residuals can mask early intolerance; chest X‑ray may miss subtle tube misplacement.
b: Albumin <3.5 g/dL may be acute phase reactant
Chest X‑ray may not show small tube kinks

faq.q: When should enteral feeding be delayed in a postoperative patient?
faq.a: If the patient has ileus, uncontrolled bleeding, or a high-output fistula, delay until the gut is functional.

faq.q: What is the first step if a nasogastric tube is suspected to be misplaced?
faq.a: Obtain a plain abdominal X‑ray to confirm position before continuing feeding.

faq.q: Why is thiamine given with enteral feeding?
faq.a: To prevent Wernicke’s encephalopathy, especially in patients with alcohol use or malnutrition.

exam: A 65‑year‑old post‑operative patient develops abdominal distension and vomiting after starting EN. What is the most likely complication and next step? — Aspiration risk; check tube position and stop feeding temporarily.
A patient with severe burns is started on EN but develops diarrhea. What is the likely cause and how to manage? — Hyperosmolar feeds; reduce osmolarity or switch to a low‑osmolar formula.
Why is early EN preferred over TPN in low‑resource settings? — Preserves gut mucosa, reduces infection risk, and is cheaper.
A nasojejunal tube is placed but the patient has persistent high gastric residuals. What does this indicate? — Possible tube misplacement or delayed gastric emptying; confirm position.
What is the contraindication for EN in a patient with suspected bowel ischemia? — Non‑functional gut; EN should be avoided until ischemia is ruled out.
When should you stop EN and switch to TPN? — If the patient develops severe aspiration pneumonia or cannot tolerate any enteral nutrition for >48 h.
